name: CartBoss
what: A pay-as-you-go tool that sends text-message reminders to shoppers who left items in their cart on Shopify and WooCommerce stores.
title: CartBoss: $73K in 30 days from texting people who forgot their cart
dek: A small Slovenian team charges stores per text message instead of a monthly fee. Revenue has swung from $27K to $72K a month in 2026. Note: TrustMRR shows MRR (monthly recurring revenue, money from subscriptions) as $0 because nobody pays a subscription.

hero.title: A no-subscription SMS tool collected $1.8M since it connected to Stripe
tags: Charge for use, not for a seat

pattern: Charge per use instead of a monthly plan

numbers.label: Verified
numbers.note: Pay-as-you-go, so TrustMRR counts no subscriptions.

series.label: Verified
series.alt: Monthly revenue falls from $43K to $35K, climbs to $53K by July, drops to $27K in September, then jumps to $72K in November (month not finished).

phases.name: The problem
phases.title: CartBoss: most people leave without paying
phases.dek: The team saw that shoppers often fill a cart and leave. They built a text message that brings them back.
phases.story:
Online stores lose a lot of sales at checkout. Someone adds shoes to their cart, gets distracted and closes the tab. That is called an abandoned cart.

The team behind CartBoss, a Slovenian company, says they spotted this as a big problem for stores and built a text-message (SMS) reminder for it. TrustMRR lists the company as founded in March 2021.

Texts get read faster than email, so a reminder can land while the shopper still remembers the cart. The company says it only sends texts, no email.
phases.lesson: Pick one leak in a business, like checkout, and fix only that.

phases.name: Launch
phases.title: CartBoss: no monthly fee, pay for each text
phases.dek: The Shopify app launched in December 2021 with a simple price: free to install, pay for each message.
phases.story:
The Shopify listing says the app launched on December 22, 2021. Its pricing line reads: pay per text message, $0 monthly fees.

That makes it easy to try. A tiny store pays a little and a big store pays more, with no plan to pick. The homepage also offers a free trial with no credit card and says the first recovered cart is free.

By September 2022 a news site reported the tool was in over 4,000 online shops and had over 500 customers, with message templates in 30 languages.

receipts.text: The Shopify listing says the app launched on Dec 22 2021 and is priced per text message with no monthly fee.
receipts.caption: Shopify App Store listing
receipts.label: Live

phases.lesson: If a customer can start for nearly nothing, you remove the biggest reason to say no.
phases.why: The trade-off is that revenue moves with how many texts stores send, which is not as steady as subscriptions.

phases.name: Proof
phases.title: CartBoss: the results people quote
phases.dek: The company shares big numbers. They come from the company and its users, not from the payment data.
phases.story:
In a podcast interview a co-founder said the tool sets up with two default abandoned-cart messages once installed and has around 15 ready-made messages in different languages.

The interview page also quotes users with an ROI (money earned compared with money spent) as high as 7,400% and click rates of 55%. It says the unsubscribe rate is typically under 1%. No method is given for how these were measured, so treat them as marketing claims.

The homepage says over 7 million carts have been recovered. The same page's heading says 7 million lost sales, so the two do not match exactly.

A May 2022 podcast page quotes lower figures: at least 2,400% ROI and about 40% click rate on the first text.

number.label: Claimed
number.source: E-commerce Fastlane podcast, episode 334 (page opens in a browser; it blocks automatic link checks)

phases.lesson: A company's own results are a starting point. Look for numbers someone else can check.

phases.name: Today
phases.title: CartBoss: a dip, then the biggest month
phases.dek: Stripe data shows revenue between $35K and $53K a month, a drop in autumn, then a jump in November.
phases.story:
TrustMRR reads CartBoss's payments straight from Stripe. From December 2025 it shows $35K to $43K a month through spring, then $50K to $53K in summer.

September and October fell to $27K and $29K. November is already $72K with days left, and the last 30 days total $73K. TrustMRR also shows 30-day growth of +163%.

We couldn't verify why. A pay-as-you-go tool can swing with how many texts stores send, for example around holiday sales, but no source says that is the cause here.

All-time, TrustMRR shows $1.84M since the account connected, and a 45% profit margin for the last 30 days as entered on the profile.
phases.lesson: With pay-as-you-go, one month can look great or bad. Compare many months.

steal.title: Steal this: price by use
items: Ask if your customers would prefer to pay only when they use it.
Offer the first result free, like the first recovered cart.
Track revenue by month, not by single days.

fact_checks.found: The homepage heading says sales, but the stat under it says 7 million carts recovered. They are not the same thing, and no method is shown.
fact_checks.label: Sources differ

fact_checks.claim: How good is the return on the texts?
fact_checks.found: The 2026-dated Fastlane page says ROI as high as 7,400% and a 55% click rate. A May 2022 podcast page says at least 2,400% ROI and about 40% on the first text. Neither explains how it was measured.
fact_checks.label: Sources differ

fact_checks.found: TrustMRR shows 0 active subscriptions and $0 MRR, yet $73K revenue in the last 30 days. That fits pay-as-you-go pricing where stores buy texts instead of subscribing.
fact_checks.label: Verified

checklist: Find an online store you like and add something to the cart. Don't buy. See which emails or texts arrive.
Write down three reasons you've left a cart before.
Sketch a price that charges per use for something you could sell.
Work out what one free first result could be in your own idea.
Look up TrustMRR and read one company's monthly revenue table.
Note one number from a company homepage and list how you could check it.
